one_liner: llama.cpp-derived CPU/GPU hybrid LLM engine that exploits ReLU activation sparsity; up to 11.69x llama.cpp on one RTX 4090.
what_it_does: Runs LLM inference on a PC with one consumer GPU when the model does not fit in VRAM, e.g. Falcon-40B or Llama-2-70B FP16 on a 24 GB RTX 4090. It is a fork-in-spirit of llama.cpp (ggml, GGUF, the same main/server/batched/perplexity examples), with -ngl replaced by --vram-budget and its own 'PowerInfer GGUF' files that bundle model weights with activation predictors. It only accelerates models with ReLU, ReGLU or squared-ReLU activations (ReLU-fied Llama 2 and Falcon, ProSparse, Bamboo, TurboSparse; a separate smallthinker/ engine for SmallThinker MoE models); standard llama.cpp weights load but run without speedup.
how_it_is_fast: Neuron activations in ReLU LLMs follow a power law: a few 'hot' FFN neurons fire for most inputs while most 'cold' neurons fire rarely. PowerInfer profiles activations offline, solves an integer linear program (cvxopt GLPK, in powerinfer-py/solver.py) to place hot neurons in VRAM and leave cold ones in host RAM, then at runtime uses small per-layer MLP predictors to guess which neurons will fire and computes only those, hot ones on the GPU and cold ones on the CPU, so weights never cross PCIe per token. ggml gains neuron-aware sparse operators for this (GGML_OP_MUL_MAT_SPARSE, GGML_OP_AXPY, ggml_mul_mat_idx with sparse and GPU index tensors). The baseline loses because llama.cpp offloads whole layers and must run every remaining dense layer on the CPU.
when_to_use: Single-user, batch-1 local generation on one consumer GPU (RTX 4090 24 GB, RTX 2080Ti 11 GB) with a model 2-6x larger than VRAM, such as a 40B or 70B model in FP16 or INT4.
You can use or create a ReLU-sparse model variant (ReluLLaMA, ReluFalcon, ProSparse-Llama-2, Bamboo-7B, TurboSparse) and accept its accuracy.
x86-64 hosts with AVX2 plus an NVIDIA (CUDA) or AMD (ROCm/HIP) GPU, on Linux or Windows.
Research on activation-sparsity offloading: the predictor, the ILP placement and the sparse ggml operators are all in the tree.
when_not_to_use: Mainstream dense models (Llama 3, Qwen, Mistral and other SiLU/GELU models): the FAQ says only ReLU-family activations are supported, and llama.cpp weights give no gain.
Accuracy-sensitive use of the 70B ReLU models: the FAQ says the ReLU fine-tune used only 5B tokens and shows a noticeable drop, worst for 70B.
Multi-GPU boxes, multi-tenant serving or high-batch throughput: multi-GPU is an open TODO and the published speedups are for single-request generation.
Apple Silicon: CPU-only on macOS, where the README says the improvement 'is not significant', and the Metal backend is still a TODO.

Projects that need upstream llama.cpp features: the ggml/llama.cpp base is a late-2023 snapshot and the engine code has seen little change since 2024 (recent commits are README edits plus the 2025 SmallThinker drop).

integration.form: static lib + CLI binaries (CMake build of a llama.cpp-style tree: main, server, quantize, batched, perplexity)
integration.dependencies: CUDA toolkit with cuBLAS (-DLLAMA_CUBLAS=ON) or ROCm hipBLAS (-DLLAMA_HIPBLAS=ON) for GPU builds; Python 3.8+ with the powerinfer helper package (torch>=2, cvxopt 1.3.2) for GPU-split solving, plus numpy, sentencepiece, transformers and gguf-py for weight conversion; the smallthinker/ engine needs clang-21 and mold
integration.min_toolchain: C11 / C++11, CMake 3.17+ (README; the top-level CMakeLists declares 3.13 and raises it to 3.17 for CUDA)
integration.platforms: x86-64 with AVX2 on Linux and Windows, with or without NVIDIA or AMD GPUs; Apple M-series CPU-only on macOS without significant gains
integration.thread_safety: not documented (inherits llama.cpp's per-context model: one llama_context per thread of generation)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same CLI and examples as llama.cpp with --vram-budget instead of -ngl, but it needs PowerInfer GGUF files with predictors and activation statistics, and runs only ReLU-family models fast

gotchas: FFN splitting fails quietly: if the powerinfer Python module or the model's activation/ directory is missing, no GPU index is generated and generation falls back to slow mode (see issue #131, 'Activation_32 Not Found (Very slow inference)'); check the log for 'offloaded ... MiB of FFN weights to GPU'.

The generated .gpuidx placement is cached next to the model; after changing VRAM budget or hardware, a stale cache can cause CUDA_ERROR_OUT_OF_MEMORY, fixed with --reset-gpu-index, a lower --vram-budget or --disable-gpu-index (FAQ).
LLAMA_NATIVE defaults to ON (-march=native), so binaries built on one CPU may not run on another.
Dense GGUFs from convert-dense.py may not work in llama.cpp because the activations (ReluLLaMA, ProSparse) or the architecture (Bamboo) were changed.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick PowerInfer over ik_llama.cpp, llamafile tinyBLAS, T-MAC or BitNet when the bottleneck is a model larger than your GPU's VRAM and you can run a ReLU-sparse variant: those siblings speed up dense or low-bit matmuls on the CPU, while PowerInfer avoids computing most FFN neurons at all. For standard dense models, or CPU-only machines, ik_llama.cpp or llamafile are the better choice.
verified_claims_summary: Per the README and the SOSP '24 paper, PowerInfer vs llama.cpp (late-2023 version) on one RTX 4090 with FP16 ReLU models (input length 64) reaches up to 11x on Falcon(ReLU)-40B and up to 3x on Llama(ReLU)-2-70B, averaging 13.20 tokens/s (peak 29.08) and up to 11.69x across models including OPT-175B; on an RTX 2080Ti with INT4 models (input length 8) it reaches up to 8x on Falcon-40B and 3x on Llama-2-70B. WebSearch snippets of the paper give the host as an Intel i9-13900K with 192 GB RAM (paper PDF not opened); compiler and flags are not stated, and the per-configuration numbers are only in README images.
status_note: MIT-licensed with about 9.8k stars, but now owned by Tiiny-AI, which sells hardware built on it; engine code last changed in 2025 (OPT model code on 2025-02-19, SmallThinker on 2025-07-27) with only README commits since, so 'active' overstates the core's maintenance.
